chunks: Differential pair and its tradeoffs. The question: What is a differential pair? What are some tradeoffs?
A differential pair is two wires that carry opposite versions of one signal. When one goes up, the other goes down by the same amount.
The receiver looks only at the difference between them. Noise that lands on both wires equally cancels out in that subtraction.
The price is double the pins and traces, and a need to keep the two wires closely matched.
Imagine two people holding the ends of a rope, with a flag in the middle that shows how far apart their hands are.
If a gust of wind pushes both people the same way, the gap between their hands does not change, so the flag stays put.
Only when they move in opposite directions does the flag move. The analogy breaks down if one person is delayed. Then the wind and the signal get mixed together.
Each line swings ±0. 2 volts around a 1. 2 volts common-mode level (LVDS-like). The receiver sees ±0. 4 volts of differential signal, twice the per-line swing.
The common-mode level (dashed) doesn't move: all of the information is in the difference.
Differential voltage ( V d ): V P minus V N . This is the signal. Common-mode voltage ( V cm ): the average (V P plus V N) over 2 . It carries no data.
CMRR: how strongly a receiver ignores common-mode noise, often given in dB ("How differential signals improve noise immunity").
Skew: a timing difference between the two wires of a pair.
Mode conversion: when imbalance turns some of the signal into common-mode noise ("Differential pair skew: why it matters, how to fix").
Differential impedance ( Z diff ): the impedance between the two wires, often 100 ohms ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Drive V P equals 1. 4 volts and V N equals 1. 0 volts. The receiver sees V d equals 0. 4 volts. The common-mode level is (1. 4 plus 1. 0) over 2 equals 1. 2 volts. Now 0.
5 volts of noise lands equally on both wires, so they read 1. 9 volts and 1. 5 volts. The difference is still 0. 4 volts, and only the common-mode level moved.
That is the whole idea.
"A differential pair is two complementary traces where the data is the voltage difference between them.
Noise that hits both lines equally is common-mode and gets subtracted out, the opposite currents make the pair radiate less, and you get a bigger signal difference for a given swing.

The costs are double the pins and traces, strict length matching and constant spacing, differential termination, and the fact that any skew converts signal into common-mode noise, so it must be routed carefully."
